---
title: "Labeling text with written rules"
subtitle: "Measure rule coverage, conflicts, and mistakes"
description: "Learn how rule-based weak labels can expand workforce training data without becoming ground truth."
categories: [training data, weak supervision, workforce research]
---

Five fictional sentence variants remain marked as synthetic. For the rule
test, the Riverton Workforce Lab returns to its 28 reviewed fictional text
units. Several phrases appear repeatedly: `training`, `required`, `shift`,
and `skill`. The team writes rules from those patterns, then examines whether
familiar words preserve distinctions a worker may use when comparing notices.

**Rule-based training data** uses written conditions to assign labels.
These proposed labels are often called **weak labels** because a rule is an
imperfect source of supervision. The team will measure where its rules label,
abstain, conflict, and disagree with human judgments.

::: {.callout-note}
The sentences and team are fictional. The author designed the rules after
examining this teaching dataset. Results on these rows are not an independent
performance estimate.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- express labeling rules as text patterns.
- preserve individual votes and conflicts.
- calculate coverage, conflict, and abstention.
- report each rule's own coverage and error.
- compare usable weak labels with reference labels.
- run rule checks on cases outside their design examples.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Write rules that can abstain

Each rule searches for words associated with one codebook category.
A rule returns `TRUE` when it votes for its category and `FALSE` otherwise.
The next chunk loads file, table, reshaping, repetition, string, and agreement
helpers. It then reads the file with declared column types.
`map()` makes one TRUE/FALSE list per rule.
`as_tibble()` converts those lists into columns.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(foundryR)

workforce_sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

rule_patterns <- c(
  training = str_c(
    "training",
    "certificat",
    "apprenticeship",
    "mentor",
    sep = "|"
  ),
  requirement = str_c(
    "required",
    "preferred",
    "license",
    "diploma",
    "portfolio",
    "must be able",
    sep = "|"
  ),
  schedule = "schedule|shift|classes",
  skill = "skill|spreadsheet|communication"
)
rule_labels <- names(rule_patterns)
sentence_text_lower <- str_to_lower(workforce_sentences$text)

rule_votes <- bind_cols(
  tibble(sentence_id = workforce_sentences$sentence_id),
  as_tibble(
    map(rule_patterns, \(pattern) {
      str_detect(sentence_text_lower, pattern)
    })
  )
)

head(rule_votes, 8)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    dim(rule_votes[rule_labels]),
    c(28L, 4L)
  ),
  identical(
    names(rule_votes[rule_labels]),
    rule_labels
  )
)
```

The rule-vote tibble preserves one column per rule. Combining the votes too
early would hide why a label was proposed.

## Mark abstentions and conflicts

A row can receive:

- one vote, which produces a usable weak label.
- no votes, which produces an abstention.
- several votes, which produces a conflict.

```{r}
rule_counts <- rule_votes |>
  mutate(
    rule_count = as.integer(rowSums(rule_votes[rule_labels]))
  ) |>
  select(sentence_id, rule_count)
voted_labels <- rule_votes |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(rule_labels),
    names_to = "weak_label",
    values_to = "rule_vote"
  ) |>
  filter(rule_vote) |>
  summarise(
    voted_label = first(weak_label),
    .by = sentence_id
  )

weak_results <- workforce_sentences |>
  select(sentence_id, text, reference_label) |>
  left_join(rule_counts, by = join_by(sentence_id)) |>
  left_join(voted_labels, by = join_by(sentence_id)) |>
  mutate(
    weak_label = case_when(
      rule_count == 0L ~ "abstain",
      rule_count > 1L ~ "conflict",
      TRUE ~ voted_label
    )
  ) |>
  select(-voted_label)

result_order <- c(
  "abstain",
  "conflict",
  "requirement",
  "schedule",
  "skill",
  "training"
)
result_counts <- tibble(weak_label = result_order) |>
  left_join(
    weak_results |>
      count(weak_label, name = "rows"),
    by = join_by(weak_label)
  ) |>
  mutate(rows = coalesce(rows, 0L))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  weak_results |>
    filter(weak_label %in% c("abstain", "conflict")),
  col.names = c(
    "Sentence ID",
    "Text",
    "Reference label",
    "Rule votes",
    "Weak-label result"
  ),
  caption = "Five text units with no rule vote or conflicting votes",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    result_counts$rows,
    c(3L, 2L, 8L, 4L, 3L, 8L)
  )
)
```

Three sentences receive no vote. Two receive conflicting votes. Sentence
`s013`, for example, contains both `certificate` and `preferred`, so the
training and requirement rules disagree.

## Report coverage before accuracy

**Coverage** is the share of rows receiving at least one vote. **Conflict
rate** is the share receiving more than one. **Usable coverage** counts rows
with exactly one vote.

```{r}
rule_summary <- tibble(
  measure = c(
    "coverage",
    "conflict rate",
    "usable coverage"
  ),
  value = c(
    mean(weak_results$rule_count > 0L),
    mean(weak_results$rule_count > 1L),
    mean(weak_results$rule_count == 1L)
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  rule_summary |>
    mutate(
      value = round(value, 3)
    ),
  col.names = c("Measure", "Share of 28 text units"),
  caption = "Coverage and conflict in the teaching dataset",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(
    all.equal(
      rule_summary$value,
      c(25 / 28, 2 / 28, 23 / 28)
    )
  )
)
```

Coverage alone does not measure correctness. A rule can label every row and be
wrong every time.

## Compare usable labels with human judgments

The 23 rows with one rule vote include two errors. We can summarize that
comparison with foundryR.

```{r}
agreement_data <- weak_results |>
  filter(rule_count == 1L) |>
  select(weak_label, reference_label)
error_sentences <- weak_results |>
  filter(
    rule_count == 1L,
    weak_label != reference_label
  )
error_sentence_ids <- error_sentences$sentence_id
rule_agreement <- foundryR::foundry_agreement(
  agreement_data,
  estimate = "weak_label",
  truth = "reference_label"
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  rule_agreement,
  col.names = c("Measure", "Value", "Compared text units"),
  caption = "In-sample agreement for usable weak labels",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(agreement_data), 23L),
  isTRUE(
    all.equal(
      filter(rule_agreement, metric == "accuracy")$value,
      21 / 23
    )
  ),
  identical(error_sentence_ids, c("s023", "s024"))
)
```

The rule labels 21 of the 23 usable rows the same way as the reference
annotation. It incorrectly labels `RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE` as `skill` and
`DATA SUPPORT CERTIFICATE` as `training`. The trigger words are present, but
the headings alone do not make either claim.

The full accounting keeps that error beside unresolved rows.

```{r}
all_row_accounting <- tibble(
  outcome = c(
    "usable and matches reference",
    "usable and differs from reference",
    "unresolved: abstain or conflict"
  ),
  rows = c(
    weak_results |>
      filter(
        rule_count == 1L,
        weak_label == reference_label
      ) |>
      nrow(),
    weak_results |>
      filter(
        rule_count == 1L,
        weak_label != reference_label
      ) |>
      nrow(),
    weak_results |>
      filter(rule_count != 1L) |>
      nrow()
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  all_row_accounting,
  col.names = c("Outcome", "Text units"),
  caption = "Accounting for all 28 rule results",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    all_row_accounting$rows,
    c(21L, 2L, 5L)
  ),
  identical(
    sum(all_row_accounting$rows),
    28L
  )
)
```

These are in-sample results. The author wrote the rules after reading the
sentences. The rules may therefore encode those examples rather than the
broader concept.

## Examine each rule separately

The pooled 21-of-23 figure conceals differences between individual rules.
Each rule has separate coverage and error counts.
Errors can differ between rows with one matching rule and rows with several
matching rules.

```{r}
reference_labels <- workforce_sentences$reference_label
votes_per_row <- as.integer(
  rowSums(rule_votes[rule_labels])
)

rule_diagnostics <- map(
  rule_labels,
  \(rule_name) {
    fired <- rule_votes[[rule_name]]
    fired_alone <- fired & votes_per_row == 1L
    matches_reference <- reference_labels == rule_name

    tibble(
      rule = rule_name,
      rows_fired = sum(fired),
      rows_fired_alone = sum(fired_alone),
      alone_and_correct = sum(fired_alone & matches_reference),
      correct_whenever_fired = sum(fired & matches_reference)
    )
  }
) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(
    precision_when_alone = alone_and_correct / rows_fired_alone
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  rule_diagnostics |>
    mutate(
      precision_when_alone = round(
        precision_when_alone,
        2
      )
    ) |>
    select(
      rule,
      rows_fired,
      rows_fired_alone,
      alone_and_correct,
      precision_when_alone
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Rule",
    "Matching rows",
    "Rows matching only this rule",
    "Correct labels when only this rule matched",
    "Precision when only this rule matched"
  ),
  caption = "Each rule's coverage and error, separated",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    rule_diagnostics$rows_fired,
    c(9L, 10L, 5L, 3L)
  ),
  identical(
    rule_diagnostics$rows_fired_alone,
    c(8L, 8L, 4L, 3L)
  ),
  identical(
    rule_diagnostics$alone_and_correct,
    c(7L, 8L, 4L, 2L)
  ),
  identical(
    sum(rule_diagnostics$rows_fired_alone),
    23L
  ),
  identical(
    sum(rule_diagnostics$alone_and_correct),
    21L
  ),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    rule_diagnostics$precision_when_alone,
    c(7 / 8, 1, 1, 2 / 3)
  ))
)
```

The `requirement` and `schedule` rules correctly labeled every row where each
was the only matching rule. The `training` rule made one error in eight such
rows. The `skill` rule matched only three rows and made one error.
Precision of two thirds on three rows indicates a problem, not established
performance on new data.

In-sample results with few matches provide little evidence of performance on
new data. Such results cannot show whether absent cases would cause errors.

## Separate conflicts from correlated same-label votes

Several rules can match one row with conflicting labels or repeated evidence.
Those cases have different consequences. The following example contains
opposing-label conflicts. It does not estimate correlation or demonstrate
confidence inflation.

```{r}
vote_matrix <- as.matrix(rule_votes[rule_labels])
rule_pairs <- expand.grid(
  first = rule_labels,
  second = rule_labels,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(first < second) |>
  mutate(
    fired_together = map2_int(
      first,
      second,
      \(left, right) {
        sum(vote_matrix[, left] & vote_matrix[, right])
      }
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(fired_together), first, second)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  rule_pairs,
  col.names = c("Rule", "Other rule", "Rows matching both rules"),
  caption = "Rows with matches from each rule pair",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(rule_pairs), 6L),
  identical(
    sum(rule_pairs$fired_together),
    2L
  ),
  identical(
    rule_pairs$fired_together[
      rule_pairs$first == "requirement" &
        rule_pairs$second == "training"
    ],
    1L
  ),
  identical(
    rule_pairs$fired_together[
      rule_pairs$first == "requirement" &
        rule_pairs$second == "schedule"
    ],
    1L
  )
)
```

Only two rule pairs match the same row, producing the two observed conflicts.
In `s013`, `certificate` matches the training pattern and `preferred` matches
the requirement pattern. In `s020`, the required shift matches both requirement
and schedule patterns.

These overlaps are conflicts, not duplicate votes for one label.
Correlated same-label votes occur when two rules tend to propose one label from
shared evidence. Two training rules with nearly identical keyword lists would
provide an example. A label model can estimate rule accuracy and dependence
under stronger data and modeling assumptions. This table does not supply that
evidence.

This lesson does not fit a label model.
Four rules, 28 rows, and two conflicting overlaps provide insufficient
information for accuracy and correlation estimates. The lesson measures rule
agreement, conflict, and abstention only.

### Examine a conflict policy

A team that needs a label for every row usually writes a priority order.
The following example applies one such order.

```{r}
priority_order <- c(
  "schedule",
  "requirement",
  "training",
  "skill"
)

resolve_by_priority <- function(row_votes) {
  chosen <- priority_order[priority_order %in% rule_labels[row_votes]]

  if (length(chosen) == 0L) {
    NA_character_
  } else {
    chosen[1]
  }
}

conflict_rows <- which(votes_per_row > 1L)
conflict_outcomes <- tibble(
  sentence_id = rule_votes$sentence_id[conflict_rows],
  reference_label = reference_labels[conflict_rows],
  resolved_label = map_chr(
    conflict_rows,
    \(row) resolve_by_priority(vote_matrix[row, ])
  )
) |>
  mutate(policy_agrees = resolved_label == reference_label)

abstain_rows <- which(votes_per_row == 0L)
abstain_outcomes <- tibble(
  sentence_id = rule_votes$sentence_id[abstain_rows],
  reference_label = reference_labels[abstain_rows]
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  conflict_outcomes,
  col.names = c(
    "Sentence ID",
    "Reference label",
    "Priority policy label",
    "Policy agrees"
  ),
  caption = "What a priority order does with the two conflicts",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  abstain_outcomes,
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Reference label"),
  caption = "Reference labels for the three rows with no rule vote",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(conflict_outcomes), 2L),
  identical(
    conflict_outcomes$sentence_id,
    c("s013", "s020")
  ),
  identical(
    conflict_outcomes$resolved_label,
    c("requirement", "schedule")
  ),
  all(conflict_outcomes$policy_agrees),
  identical(nrow(abstain_outcomes), 3L),
  all(abstain_outcomes$reference_label == "other")
)
```

The policy resolves both conflicts correctly, but this provides little
performance evidence. The author chose the order after reading the codebook's
timing-priority rule. Evaluation used only two rows.
Those two successes do not establish performance on new data.

All three rows with complete abstention have the reference label `other`.
No rule targets that category, so abstention is appropriate.
A separate keyword rule for `other` would be less appropriate.
The codebook assigns `other` in the absence of the four other categories, not
by particular words.

The accounting includes all 28 rows.
Twenty-one usable labels match the reference, and two differ.
A stated policy resolves two conflicts. Three abstentions have reference
labels outside the rule set. No rows remain unreported.

## Examine cases outside the rule-design examples

Before another batch, the team writes four fictional adversarial unit tests.
The team chooses expected labels after rule design to expose known rule
limitations. These cases are not an independent evaluation sample.

```{r}
stress_cases <- tibble(
  case_id = sprintf("challenge-%d", 1:4),
  text = c(
    "The training department is hiring an accountant.",
    "Employees learn from experienced coworkers.",
    "Certification is not required.",
    "Flexible hours are available."
  ),
  reference_label = c(
    "other",
    "training",
    "requirement",
    "schedule"
  ),
  reference_status = "designed challenge expectation"
)

stress_text_lower <- str_to_lower(stress_cases$text)
stress_votes <- bind_cols(
  tibble(case_id = stress_cases$case_id),
  as_tibble(
    map(rule_patterns, \(pattern) {
      str_detect(stress_text_lower, pattern)
    })
  )
)
stress_counts <- stress_votes |>
  mutate(
    rule_count = as.integer(rowSums(stress_votes[rule_labels]))
  ) |>
  select(case_id, rule_count)
stress_voted_labels <- stress_votes |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(rule_labels),
    names_to = "weak_label",
    values_to = "rule_vote"
  ) |>
  filter(rule_vote) |>
  summarise(
    voted_label = first(weak_label),
    .by = case_id
  )

stress_results <- stress_cases |>
  left_join(stress_counts, by = join_by(case_id)) |>
  left_join(stress_voted_labels, by = join_by(case_id)) |>
  mutate(
    weak_label = case_when(
      rule_count == 0L ~ "abstain",
      rule_count > 1L ~ "conflict",
      TRUE ~ voted_label
    )
  ) |>
  select(-rule_count, -voted_label)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  stress_results,
  col.names = c(
    "Challenge ID",
    "Challenge text",
    "Reference label",
    "Reference status",
    "Rule result"
  ),
  caption = "Four designed adversarial failures",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    stress_results$weak_label,
    c("training", "abstain", "conflict", "abstain")
  ),
  !any(
    stress_results$weak_label == stress_results$reference_label
  )
)
```

`training department` triggers a false positive. `Employees learn` and
`Flexible hours` use words the rules do not cover. `Certification is not
required` creates a conflict. These failures reveal missing context, synonyms,
and negation.

## Keep weak labels weak

When applying rules to more data:

1. version every pattern and codebook.
2. preserve each rule vote and abstention.
3. measure coverage and conflict by source, language, and group.
4. reserve independently reviewed data for evaluation.
5. sample apparent successes for human audit.
6. run checks for negation, polysemy, and unseen wording.
7. compare conclusions with and without weak labels.

Rules can provide useful training signals. They do not create facts, repair a
source's systematic errors, or remove the need for people who understand the domain.

## What to remember

- A weak label is a rule's proposal, not ground truth.
- Rules should permit abstention and show conflicts.
- Coverage, conflict, and agreement answer different questions.
- Report each rule separately. A pooled score hides weaker rules.
- Rules that share trigger words are not independent votes.
- In-sample success can reflect rules written around the examples.
- Designed challenge cases expose known limitations.
- Independent evaluation measures rule performance on new data.

The investigation asks what each fictional notice explicitly states about
training, schedules, requirements, and skills. The Lab can trace each answer
through the source, OCR checks, codebook, individual labels, synthetic status,
and rule votes. Those records do not make the notices representative or
establish rule performance on new data. They make limits and unresolved cases
available for inspection.
